videos.title: Is Ireland ready to steer the EU council presidency?
videos.transcript: A lot of preparation has gone into taking over this presidency. We're talking about years, years in the making, not just from the point of view of human resources in the Irish permanent representation, which is basically the civil service now on steroids out here in Brussels, but also in terms of resources like buildings and building up every level, whether it's making sure that the Irish language is fully recognized and fully to the forefront during the presidency because this is our first presidency since Ireland and Irish Gaelic has got its official status. >> But they maintain the focus on security and defense because that is vital. So, the teams of the Irish presidency are in alignment, very much in alignment with the Cypriot presidency because we are talking about competitiveness, we are talking about security and defense, and our third priority then is values.
videos.summary: The video discusses Ireland's preparations for taking over the EU Council presidency, highlighting years of planning and the significance of Irish Gaelic gaining official EU status. A spokesperson outlines the presidency's three main priorities: competitiveness, security and defense, and values. Ireland's agenda is described as closely aligned with the preceding Cypriot presidency.

videos.title: How has Brexit changed Britain’s economy?  | The Economist
videos.transcript: How exactly has Brexit changed Britain's economy? It's been ten years since Britain decided to leave the European Union The dawn is breaking on an independent United Kingdom The country has been through six prime ministers since then and is now more divided, less influential and poorer than it otherwise might have been Brexit was a huge mistake Most economists agree that Brexit has damaged the economy Some say GDP per person is 8% lower, while others say it's only 2.5% We may not know the exact cost, but what we do know is that growth in most other big, rich countries has been faster than in Britain The effects are clearest in manufacturing Brexiteers promise to free Britain from the shackles of EU regulations They said that any trade losses with the EU would be more than made up for by greater trade with the rest of the world But that's not what's happened The value in real terms of goods traded with the EU has fallen by 7% since 2016 But trade with the rest of the world has also fallen by 6% Competition from China and high energy costs were already making life harder for British manufacturing But Brexit sped up its decline by introducing new barriers to trade with the EU, such as extra border checks and more paperwork Over 16,000 British businesses have given up exporting to the EU altogether— that's 14% of all exporters to the continent But it's not all doom and gloom Britain's exports of services have actually risen since 2016 by £62bn in the EU and £107bn in the rest of the world The biggest growth in output has been in industries with few trade barriers like IT services or advertising That has happened despite Brexit, not because of it Sectors where Brexit introduced new obstacles like financial services, they've done worse But Brexit alone can't be blamed for Britain's sluggish economy It fundamentally has the same strengths and the same weaknesses as before 2016— leaving the EU has just made everything a little bit harder
videos.summary: This video marks ten years since Britain voted to leave the European Union and examines how Brexit has affected the British economy. It looks at the impact on trade, manufacturing, and services, drawing on economic data to assess what has changed since 2016. While Brexit has made some things harder, the video also notes that Britain's economic weaknesses existed before the vote.

trueFalse.statement: Britain's exports of services have risen since 2016.
Trade with the rest of the world increased after Brexit, making up for losses with the EU.
High energy costs and competition from China were already putting pressure on British manufacturing before Brexit.

ordering.instruction: Put these events or developments in the order they are mentioned in the video.
items: Britain votes to leave the European Union
New trade barriers such as extra border checks are introduced with the EU
Over 16,000 British businesses stop exporting to the EU
Britain's exports of services rise, with the biggest growth in IT and advertising

videos.title: South Korea unveils $576 billion AI chip investment
videos.transcript: South Korea rolled out sweeping chip and AI mega projects on Monday. >> President Lee Jang pledged investments worth more than $576 billion over several years. It's a move that aims to cement the nation's overwhelming industry leadership. Lee was joined for the announcement by the leaders of Samsung Electronics and SKH Highix. High bandwidth memory chips produced by both tech giants have become pivotal in the global race to build advanced AI systems. Lee said the world's two largest memory chip makers will invest around 518 billion with suppliers to build two new chip fabrication sites each in South Korea's southwest region. He announced plans for the southwest to host major chip production clusters drawing on abundant underused power. Lee defended these proposed new hubs over the weekend as a national survival strategy to ease regional imbalances and expand capacity for the AI era. Representatives of other firms including LG Electronics and HD Hyundai Robotics also attended.
videos.summary: South Korea has announced a massive investment plan worth over $576 billion in chip manufacturing and artificial intelligence. President Lee Jang made the announcement alongside leaders from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, outlining plans to build new chip fabrication sites in the country's southwest region. The initiative is described as a national survival strategy to boost capacity for the AI era and reduce regional imbalances.

videos.title: Is getting a 2nd passport the hot new accessory?
videos.transcript: I'm lucky to have two passports, and apparently more US Americans are catching on at record numbers. While claiming a second citizenship used to be about identity and nationality, it seems to have become more about having a backup plan, whether due to burnout from the American working culture, politics, fear of violence, [music] or the romanticization of the European lifestyle. >> For breakfast, we do something cool like have a cigarette, then we go for work for like 1 1/2 hour to 1/2 hour. >> common route is claiming citizenship via ancestry. Some countries have golden passport programs, where investing enough money into the economy can get you citizenship, [music] or through residency, living somewhere legally long enough to be eligible to apply. But, there is pushback. A bill was introduced in the US [music] Senate that would force Americans to hold only one passport. Though legal experts say it's almost [music] certainly unconstitutional and won't pass. Would you consider getting a second passport?

videos.title: Why is the UK not built for extreme heat? #Heatwave #UK #Weather #Climate #BBCNews
videos.transcript: Why is the UK just not built for extreme weather? We're just at the start of what's going to be an intense heat wave. But the reality is that the average summer temperature here is just about 16° C. With those mostly mild conditions, we're building for those conditions instead. But the future is going to be much hotter and much wetter. Large parts of our train network run on electricity and power lines sag in high temperatures. So that can mean trains get cancelled. We've also built our towns and cities with lots of rock and concrete. It absorbs the heat and then radiates it back out, making that heat even more unbearable. We're also building lots of shiny new apartments with lots of glass, which traps the heat, just like a greenhouse. And it may come as a surprise to those people not living here, but only about 5% of homes in the UK have air conditioning. All this means is that so far we haven't adapted our lives to extreme heat in the way many other countries already
videos.summary: This video explains why the UK is poorly prepared for extreme heat waves. It looks at how the country's infrastructure, buildings, and low rates of air conditioning make hot weather especially difficult to cope with. The video also points out that the UK will need to adapt as temperatures rise in the future.
